meta.title: Who really said "I do not wish women to have power over men, but over themselves"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Mary Wollstonecraft wrote it in A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), ch. IV. The original says "them," not "women." Often misattributed to Mary Shelley.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I do not wish women to have power over men, but over themselves'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Mary Wollstonecraft, 1792, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman ch. IV. The original wording is "them," lightly modernized to "women." Not Mary Shelley.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From “A Vindication of the Rights of Woman” (1792), Chapter IV. Answering Rousseau, Wollstonecraft wrote: “This is the very point I aim at. I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.” The popular version simply swaps the pronoun “them” for “women” and softens the semicolon to a comma — a light modernization of a genuine line.

source.excerpt: ‘Educate women like men,’ says Rousseau, ‘and the more they resemble our sex the less power will they have over us.’ This is the very point I aim at. I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.
trail: The full text of Chapter IV on Wikisource contains the line verbatim: “I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.”
The quotation archive WIST logs it to “Vindication of the Rights of Woman, ch. 4 (1792)” and notes it is “typically shortened” to the “women” wording.
The line answers Rousseau directly — Wollstonecraft quotes his claim that educated women will have “less power” over men, then turns it: self-command, not dominion, is the aim.
source.excerptNote: The words in the shared quote are Wollstonecraft’s; the widely circulated form replaces “them” with “women” and a semicolon with a comma.
source.rightsNote: “A Vindication of the Rights of Woman” was first published in 1792, so both the original text and this passage are firmly in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
author.heading: About Mary Wollstonecraft
author.bio: Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer and philosopher whose 1792 treatise A Vindication of the Rights of Woman is a founding text of feminist thought, arguing that women appear inferior only because they are denied education. She died in 1797, days after giving birth to Mary Shelley, the future author of Frankenstein — a family link that fuels the frequent misattribution of this very quote.

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly credited to
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Wollstonecraft is correct, but two things go astray online: who said it, and its exact words.

items.why: The line is regularly credited to Mary Shelley — Wollstonecraft’s daughter — including on a widely shared Goodreads quote page and various blogs. Shelley was an infant when her mother died in 1797 and never wrote it; the mother-daughter connection simply invites the mix-up.

Wollstonecraft’s original says “I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves” (per Wikisource, ch. IV). The circulating form replaces “them” with “women” and the semicolon with a comma — a faithful modernization, not a distortion of meaning.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Mary Wollstonecraft’s, written in 1792 in Chapter IV of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman — not Mary Shelley’s, and only lightly reworded.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Wollstonecraft frames the line as a direct rebuttal to Rousseau, who had argued that educating women would only make them “resemble our sex” and so lose their power over men. Her answer inverts the whole premise: the goal is not for women to rule men, but to govern themselves — autonomy, not dominion.
The sentiment recurs across the book. A chapter later she presses the same idea in different words: women should contend for equality, “not empire.”
context.pull: Not power over men — power over themselves.
